strengths: Significant dataset contribution: EEmoDB is the largest AICA instruction dataset with 1.23M QA pairs and 36k curated samples, carefully constructed with thoughtful label refinement (synonym mapping, VAD-based clustering, expert-grounded reasoning generation)

Comprehensive evaluation framework: Benchmarks against 23 baselines across 4 categories with both in-domain (EEmo-Bench) and cross-domain evaluation (Artphoto, ArtEmis, UNIAA, AesBench) under zero-shot fairness constraints

Well-designed task-customized GRPO rewards: Hierarchical reward functions (format, ranking, hybrid regression, similarity) demonstrate careful engineering that balances multiple objectives simultaneously
Strong in-domain results: State-of-the-art performance on EEmo-Bench (68.54% perception, 67.97% ranking) with detailed ablation studies validating design choices

Rigorous data construction pipeline: Grounding reasoning generation in expert comments rather than pure model generation; principled handling of heterogeneous emotion taxonomies across 7 source datasets
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on automated data generation with limited validation: 97% of EEmoDB-QA is model-assisted; VAD validation uses only 180 samples; no inter-annotator agreement reported for EEmoDB-Assess curated set

Limited technical novelty: Two-stage SFT+GRPO is standard; novelty reduces to engineering task-specific rewards that are combinations of existing metrics (margin scaling, distance measures) rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation
Modest cross-domain generalization: Only 2.1% improvement over EmoCaliber on Artphoto (42.43% vs 40.32%) and 1.9% on ArtEmis (35.10% vs 33.23%); no statistical significance testing provided

Unexplained design choices and missing ablations: No sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters (λbase, λpeak, m, p); Table 4 row 5 shows dramatic 36% performance drop when adding all GRPO tasks without explanation; LoRA placement choice (both encoder and LLM) not justified

Evaluation protocol concerns: Using Deepseek for both annotation and evaluation creates potential circularity; probability-based conversion for baselines vs direct prediction for EEmo-Logic may disadvantage comparisons; no confidence intervals or significance testing

Data quality and information loss: Mapping 26 EMOTIC emotions to 7 Ekman categories causes information loss; heterogeneous source datasets acknowledged but impact not thoroughly investigated; downward emotion mapping strategy not validated
Presentation and clarity issues: Figure 2 is overly complex; critical details relegated to appendix; notation inconsistencies; 5-round Deepseek evaluation appears ad-hoc without sensitivity analysis

Limited scope and reproducibility concerns: Only tested on Qwen2.5-VL-7B; relies on proprietary models (DeepSeek, Qwen3) for generation/evaluation; code availability promised but not provided for review; computational cost analysis missing

strengths: Large-scale, well-constructed dataset (1.23M instructions) that consolidates categorical and dimensional emotion paradigms—addresses real gap in AICA corpus for MLLM training
Rigorous dataset construction with systematic label refinement (synonym mapping, VAD-based clustering) and multi-layer validation (82.88% QA accuracy, Krippendorff's α)
Thoughtful two-stage framework: Stage 1 SFT for foundational QA, Stage 2 GRPO with novel task-specific rewards (hybrid regression, semantic similarity fusing VAD+embeddings)
Comprehensive evaluation: 23 baselines, in-domain (EEmo-Bench) + cross-domain (Artphoto, ArtEmis, UNIAA, AesBench) benchmarks with SOTA results (perception 70.05%, ranking 67.97%)
Strong empirical validation including 144% improvement on dominance prediction and thorough ablations justifying LoRA, two-stage approach, and GRPO components
Excellent reproducibility: 35-page supplementary material with detailed prompts, hyperparameters, semantic descriptions, and evaluation protocols; promise to release code/data
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on automated generation for 1.2M samples with limited validation (~1000 samples tested); VAD continuous validation yields modest SRCC 0.70-0.69 on only 600 samples

Label refinement methodology has arbitrary design choices: uniform contribution hypothesis for emotion probabilities (Section C.1) lacks justification; linear regression assumption for VAD clustering may oversimplify emotion geometry
Limited method novelty: backbone is existing Qwen2.5-VL-7B, SFT+GRPO is standard, main contribution is reward design which while thoughtful is incremental; LoRA fine-tuning is established practice

Comparison fairness issues: primary results (Table 1) evaluate zero-shot baselines vs. EEmo-Logic trained on EEmoDB; Table 14 partial fix but stronger baselines (e.g., Qwen3-VL-8B) not fine-tuned on EEmoDB
Insufficient failure analysis: no systematic study of failure modes; cross-domain inconsistency (ArtEmis F1 31.58% vs Artphoto 38.68%) not explained; emotion-oriented baselines surprisingly poor
Evaluation concerns: description task uses LLM judge (DeepSeek) introducing potential bias; probability-based VAD evaluation for baselines may not be fair comparison; some metric aggregations unclear
Practical deployment limitations not addressed: trained on H200 GPUs (140GB)—not widely accessible; no inference time/efficiency analysis; no guidance for real-world application selection

Data quality concerns: continuous VAD generation relies on lexicon-based approach which may miss complex nuances; potential cultural bias in emotion definitions acknowledged but not addressed; reliance on proprietary models (GPT-4V, Gemini) for reasoning generation

strengths: Comprehensive dataset aggregation from 7 existing AICA sources with unified instruction format provides practical value to community
Well-organized presentation with clear methodology pipeline (Figure 2) and extensive supplementary documentation
Thorough experimental evaluation spanning 23 baselines across multiple datasets and evaluation dimensions
Addresses important practical problem of comprehensive emotion understanding combining both CES and DES paradigms
Promising engineering of multi-task GRPO with thoughtful reward designs for different emotion assessment tasks
weaknesses: Critical unfair comparison: Main results (Tab. 1-3) compare EEmo-Logic trained on 1.2M instructions against baselines trained on different/smaller corpora. Table 14 shows fair comparison dramatically narrows the gap, suggesting most gains come from data not methodology

Serious data quality concerns from heavy LLM dependency: Descriptions (Qwen2.5), reasoning (DeepSeek), and VAD labels (lemma averaging) are all model-generated with limited human validation (only 400 of 1.2M+ pairs evaluated)
Circular reasoning problem: Model trained on LLM-generated reasoning then evaluated on reproducing similar LLM reasoning, not demonstrating genuine understanding

Marginal cross-domain performance: Artphoto 38.68% F1 vs EmoCaliber 39.37% (underperforms), ArtEmis 31.58% vs 30.59% (1% improvement), UNIAA 75.65% vs 76.72% (underperforms) - improvements within noise margins
Limited methodological novelty: Two-stage SFT+GRPO is established; reward designs are incremental combinations of existing techniques (margin functions, Gaussian kernels, similarity metrics)
Insufficient ablation studies: Limited systematic testing of hyperparameters (λbase, λpeak, σ, λsim, m, p). Data generation choices and label mapping sensitivity not explored
VAD generation quality concerns: Averaging keyword norms is crude; discrete validation (91-94% agreement) insufficient for continuous regression task; no continuous VAD reliability analysis

Problematic evaluation: Direct VAD prediction vs probability-based baselines not directly comparable; LLM-based description evaluation introduces model bias; overclaimed 'novel' rewards are routine engineering

strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: EEmoDB is the largest AICA instruction dataset to date (1.23M QA pairs from 128K images), addressing a real gap with comprehensive coverage of both CES and DES paradigms

Rigorous data construction: Systematic label refinement with human validation (94%+ agreement on VAD discretization, 82.88% QA accuracy), Krippendorff's α scores of 0.81-0.86 indicating good consistency

Strong empirical results: Achieves/approaches state-of-the-art across multiple benchmarks (EEmo-Bench, Artphoto, ArtEmis, UNIAA, AesBench) with particularly strong performance on ranking and VAD assessment
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 23 baselines across 4 categories, detailed ablation studies, both in-domain and cross-domain evaluation, and thorough component analysis
Excellent presentation and reproducibility: Well-structured writing with clear motivation, detailed supplementary materials, specific hyperparameters, and commitment to release code/data
Good cross-domain generalization: Robust zero-shot performance on unseen datasets demonstrates practical utility of the framework
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty in model design: Stage 1 uses standard LoRA fine-tuning; Stage 2 applies existing GRPO framework from Shao et al. (2024); task-specific rewards are incremental engineering rather than methodological innovation

Potential noise in dataset generation: (1) VAD generation assumes uniform emotion contribution (may not hold when annotators select fewer emotions), (2) emotion reasoning texts model-generated via DeepSeek despite grounding in comments, (3) emotion rankings derived via heuristics rather than explicit annotations

Cross-cultural and subjective limitations: Mapping diverse datasets to 7 basic emotions may lose nuance; acknowledged difficulty generalizing to abstract/cartoon/object categories suggests cultural variance in emotion perception

Evaluation methodology concerns: (1) LLM-based judge for description task introduces subjectivity despite five-round protocol, (2) comparison on EEmo-Bench conflates dataset quality with model quality, (3) some emotion-oriented baselines perform surprisingly poorly (unclear if properly configured)
Model performance gaps: Gemini-2.5-Pro leads on several subtasks; direct numerical VAD prediction shows only marginal advantage over simpler probability-based methods in some dimensions

Dataset quality assumptions not fully validated: VAD generation validation limited to discretized categories (400 samples); model-generated reasoning texts validated on only 400 QA instances; potential for systematic bias from specific LLM choices (Qwen2.5, DeepSeek)
